newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-NZ's Brash urges more fiscal restraint.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NZ's Brash urges more fiscal restraint.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash on Monday warned of problems on the fiscal front, urged spending restraint to curtail the New Zealand dollar and suggested a reconsideration of the second round of planned tax cuts.

Speaking to Federated Farmers in Invercargill, Brash said some parties in coalition talks to form a government after the inconclusive election a month ago would have to rethink the second round of a NZ$3 billion tax package due in mid-1997.
"Coalition partners may indeed need to consider deferring some part of the tax cuts already announced if there is to be any increase in government expenditure," Brash said.
Coalition talks are taking place between New Zealand First and both the National and Labour parties at the moment.
New Zealand First and Labour are promising increased social spending, but National has previously said it is committed to further tax cuts. The first round of cuts was implemented in July.
Brash said one way of reducing the risk inherent in the present situation would be to ensure that further "fiscal stimulus" was not added during the coalition process.
"There is obviously a huge problem for political leaders in this situation," he said.
"The public tends to assume that so long as there is a fiscal surplus, the government can quite prudently spend it and indeed should do so."
Brash said monetary policy had been attempting to restrain pressures in the economy, which was attempting to grow beyond its sustainable growth rate.
Much of the pressure had come via the construction sector and housing market, he said.
Brash said there was little doubt that a different distribution of gain and pain in favour of exporters would have been preferable for the sake of the long-term health of the economy.
New Zealand's high interest rates had not been high enough to deter rapid increases in borrowing. This had coincided with a rapid rise in migration over the last two years.

Fiscal policy expansion had recently contributed to the need for rather tighter monetary conditions than might otherwise be the case. This was notwithstanding that New Zealand was running the highest surplus of any country in the OECD.

"The tax reductions and expenditure increases announced in recent months amount to a substantial turnaround in the fiscal position, which has moved from a strongly rising surplus to a rather smaller one over quite a short period of time," Brash said.
"The extend of the turnaround at some four percent of GDP over two years, represents a significant reduction in fiscal policy's braking action on the economy," he said.
He said circumstances had changed since the bank approved the tax cuts in November 1995. The economy had proved more resilient in 1996 than had been expected.

"The net result has been that fiscal policy has reduced its braking action on the domestic economy at a time when the economy remains somewhat overstretched, and has thereby required montary conditions to be firmer than otherwise," Brash said.
He said perceptions about the fiscal position were also affecting the situation.
There was a wide public perception that coalition building would result in a net additional fiscal stimulus as parties seek to accommodate promises made by potential partners.
Capital flows to New Zealand, which at other times would be welcomed, were exacerbating the unfortunate distribution of gain and pain, Brash said.
"The exchange rate is pushed higher, and interest rates are pushed lower."
Brash said the present situation was a product of temporary forces, not lasting ones.

The bank's September projections indicated inflation pressures would ease over the next year to allow some easing in monetary policy. But at some stage soon, the interest rates of New Zealand's trading partners would rise and that could slow a fall in New Zealand's rates.
Brash ruled out a temporary relaxation of monetary policy. Any benefits from a lower exchange rate would be wiped out by higher inflation, he said.
He also rejected redefining the inflation target or removing the housing component from the inflation index.
"One clear way of reducing the risk inherent in the present situation would be to ensure that further fiscal stimulus is not added in the process of coalition forming," he said.
Coalition partners may need to consider deferring some part of the tax cuts already announced if there is to be any increase in government expenditure, he said.
"There is obviously a huge problem for political leaders in this situation," Brash said.
He also called for a more realistic understanding on the part of foreign investors of the risks of investing in New Zealand dollar assets.
"Unfortunately it seems to have become accepted popular wisdom both here and abroad that investing in New Zealand dollar assets has become a virtually riskless exercise," he said.

Brash said one way of reducing the risk would be to ensure that government spending did not rise as the major political parties negotiated the formation of a new government following the inconclusive general election.
